query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the spray distance on the HVAF‑i7 torch to around 300–350 mm will increase particle velocity during deposition and thereby enhance the deposition efficiency, resulting in a thicker, adherent FeCoNiCrAl bond coat that retains minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy gas‐atomized powder with a 15–45 μm size range, previously demonstrated to yield high‐quality coatings using the HVAF‐M3 configuration.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF‑i7 deposition process by increasing the spray distance to approximately 300–350 mm to boost particle velocity.
generation.conditions: Deposition on substrates (including those with internal diameters as small as 120 mm) under high‐velocity oxygen fuel spraying conditions; the resulting bond coat must perform under high‐temperature thermal-barrier service (e.g., exposure to temperatures ≥800 °C in oxidizing environments).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced kinetic energy of the particles upon impact, leading to improved in-flight particle cohesion and denser microstructure formation with superior inter-splat bonding.
generation.mechanism: Higher particle velocity (achieved by adjusting the spray distance) reduces drop-off and in-flight oxidation while increasing the energy of impact. This improvement in kinetic energy facilitates better splat flattening, stronger interlamellar bonding, and overall increased deposition efficiency, thereby allowing a thicker layer to be built without compromising coating integrity or oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline using 15–45 μm feedstock on the HVAF‑M3 torch, the optimized HVAF‑i7 setting at 300–350 mm should yield a substantially thicker coating that remains dense and adherent with similar minimal levels of as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced with the 15–45 μm feedstock using the HVAF‑M3 torch (which gave high-quality coatings) versus the inadequate thickness observed with the same feedstock on the HVAF‑i7 torch using default spray distances.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to yield improved thickness only if the higher particle velocity does not introduce excessive oxidation or compromise coating adhesion; effectiveness may be constrained by the inherent design limits of the HVAF‑i7 system and the thermal constraints of processing within small-diameter (120 mm) geometries.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative increase in thickness and the balance between increased deposition efficiency and potential oxidation effects are uncertain without further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled set of coating depositions using the HVAF‑i7 torch on identical substrates (including confined geometries with 120 mm internal diameters) while varying the spray distance (e.g., standard distance vs. 300 mm and 350 mm). For each condition, measure coating thickness, deposition efficiency, oxidation levels, microhardness, and adhesion strength.
measurements: Deposition efficiency (mass gain per unit time)
Oxidation levels (via X-ray diffraction and EDS analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If coatings deposited with the optimized spray distances (300–350 mm) do not show a statistically significant increase in thickness without degradation in oxidation resistance or adhesion relative to the baseline, or if there is a marked increase in detrimental oxidation that compromises mechanical properties, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, in-flight oxidation of the AlCoCrFeNi particle during the spraying process can be beneficial for the tribological performance of the HEA coatings. Due to high specific surface area, the powder can oxidize differently from the cast bulk alloy. Moreover, the formation of multiple oxides—alumina, chromia, and spinel—changes the residual particle’s core composition and can lead to phase destabilization. Therefore, understanding the regularity of the oxidation behavior and phase transformation of the high-entropy powder at different conditions should be necessary for the production of a coating with high and determined property levels. In this work, the oxidation behavior and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder, produced via gas atomization, were studied. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and under prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 HVOF coatings were produced using various distances from the spray nozzle to the substrate to produce coatings with different oxide contents, and the coatings’ properties were investigated.
